questions.prompt: FCFS can suffer a convoy effect when
options: A long job reaches the CPU first and short jobs wait behind it
Every job has the same burst
The quantum is one cycle
Aging is enabled
questions.explanation: First-come first-served does not look at burst length. One long job at the head of the queue delays everyone who arrived just after it.

options: Picks the ready job with the smallest burst, and can starve a long job
Always matches FCFS
Needs no idea of the burst length
Is preemptive by definition
questions.explanation: If bursts are known, SJF minimizes average waiting time for a given arrival set. A long job can wait forever if short jobs keep arriving.
traps: The average-wait claim needs burst knowledge or an estimate.

questions.prompt: If a round-robin quantum becomes tiny
options: Context-switch overhead eats the time jobs should have been running
Waiting time is always zero
The policy turns into FCFS
Starvation becomes impossible at no cost
questions.explanation: Each switch saves and restores state. If the quantum is shorter than that work, the CPU spends itself switching.

questions.prompt: Which policies can preempt a running job?
options: Round robin, when the quantum expires
Preemptive priority, when a more urgent job becomes ready
FCFS
Non-preemptive SJF
questions.explanation: FCFS and non-preemptive SJF run the chosen job to completion. Round robin and preemptive priority take the CPU back.

questions.prompt: Turnaround time of a job is
options: Completion time minus arrival time
Only the time spent waiting, with the burst excluded
The quantum
The number of context switches in the whole system
questions.explanation: Turnaround includes both waiting and running. Waiting time leaves the burst out. They are not synonyms.
traps: Using waiting time when the question says turnaround.

questions.prompt: Aging, as a fix for priority scheduling,
options: Gradually improves the priority of jobs that have waited
Deletes long jobs
Disables the clock
Sets every quantum to zero
questions.explanation: A job that sits in the queue gets a better priority over time, so a stream of urgent jobs cannot postpone it forever.

questions.prompt: Jobs P and Q arrive at time 0. P’s burst is 1 and Q’s burst is 10. FCFS runs P then Q. What is Q’s waiting time?
questions.explanation: Q waits only while P runs, so the wait is 1. Q’s turnaround is 11, which is a different question.
traps: Reporting turnaround (11) when the question asks for waiting time.

options: Spends most of its life waiting for devices, with short CPU bursts
Computes for a long time between tiny I/O waits
Never enters the waiting state
Cannot be scheduled by round robin
questions.explanation: The opposite is CPU-bound: a long compute stretch between I/O. I/O-bound jobs leave the CPU idle from their point of view while the device works.

questions.prompt: Why is “use the smallest possible quantum” not a free win for round robin?
questions.answer: Each switch has a cost in saved registers and cold caches. A tiny quantum spends the CPU on switching.
questions.explanation: The quantum should be large next to the switch cost and small enough that interactive jobs still get the CPU promptly.
